title: The Conversational AI Land Grab Is On For Customer Service
summary: CCaaS and CRM vendors are acquiring conversational AI vendors for customer service. This blurs the lines between software categories.
body_markdown:
The[conversational AI market for customer service](https://www.forrester.com/report/the-conversational-ai-platforms-for-customer-service-landscape-q4-2025/RES188659) is consolidating fast.


Here is a quick recap of the last six months: Salesforce acquired[Fin](https://investor.salesforce.com/news/news-details/2026/Salesforce-Signs-Definitive-Agreement-to-Acquire-Fin/) and[Cresta](https://www.salesforce.com/news/stories/salesforce-signs-definitive-agreement-to-acquire-cresta/) ; Five9 acquired[Level AI](https://www.five9.com/news/news-releases/five9-acquire-level-ai-advancing-ai-powered-cx-platform) ; Dialpad acquired[Ada](https://www.dialpad.com/press/dialpad-and-ada/) ; and SoundHound acquired[LivePerson](https://investors.soundhound.com/news-releases/news-release-details/soundhound-ai-completes-acquisition-liveperson-creating-world) , to name a few. And let’s not forget NiCE’s 2025 acquisition of Cognigy.


### Key Takeaways From The Conversational AI Market Consolidation


1. **CRM and CCaaS vendors are not just acquiring chatbots.** Acquired functions span voice and digital AI, real-time AI assistance, conversation intelligence, quality management, reasoning over customer context, and executing work in back-end systems. CCaaS and CRM vendors are buying the intelligence layer that increasingly determines how work gets done and how customer operations get optimized by learning from work outcomes. They are combining these capabilities into a single platform — not in a collection of discrete tools.


2. **The deals are helping blur the boundaries between CRM and CCaaS.** CRM vendors control customer data, cases, knowledge, business rules, and workflows. CCaaS vendors control voice, messaging, routing, and rich interaction data. The assets being acquired connect those two worlds. They interpret intent, determine next-best actions, assist customer service reps, orchestrate workflows, and increasingly execute actions autonomously. This reframes the old competitive battleground from who owns the customer record or communications channel to who controls the service execution layer.


3. **Acquired companies signal where the value-add is for core CRM and CCaaS technologies.** Vendors are buying capabilities that let them own more of the resolution loop, from customer intent to customer outcome. And that raises the bar for remaining independents such as Observe.AI, Parloa, or PolyAI. They will need to demonstrate differentiated capabilities that large platforms can’t easily replicate, or they will have to position themselves as an independent AI layer spanning multiple CRM and CCaaS ecosystems.


4. **For now, acquirers have an incentive to preserve conversational AI as a horizontal layer.** Five9 plans to make Level AI available across competing and on-premises contact-center environments, while Salesforce has said Cresta will continue supporting customers’ existing telephony platforms. This gives vendors an AI-first, platform-second route into accounts: enterprises can adopt AI agents, agent assistance, conversation analytics, and automated quality management without first replacing their CRM or CCaaS platform. The risk is that this openness diminishes as acquired technologies become more tightly integrated with the parent platform.


5. **These deals accelerate consumption and outcome pricing.** Traditional CRM and CCaaS vendors monetized customer service primarily by licensing human workers. And as AI does more of the work, service volume becomes less tightly linked to seats. Vendors increasingly have incentives to monetize AI through consumption or outcomes. This shifts the battleground from which vendor best equips the CSR to what combination of AI and CSR labor controls, executes, and gets paid for the work that gets done.
